<a id="pm-s1"></a>
## 1. Abstract and result contract

> We give a uniform randomized approximation scheme for unit-cost edit distance. For every fixed rational $`\varepsilon\in(0,1)`$, it estimates the distance between arbitrary explicitly stored strings of total length <i>N</i> within a factor $`1+\varepsilon`$ with probability at least 2/3, in worst-case expected time $`N^{1+o(1)}`$ on a logarithmic-word RAM. The algorithm supports polynomially bounded integer alphabets and returns zero deterministically on equal strings.

- **claim-main-approximation-scheme** (theorem, [source](#stmt-thm-main)): There is one uniform randomized algorithm that, given $x,y$ and a rational $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, returns a nonnegative integer $\widehat D$ such that $$\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\le \widehat D\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr] \ge \frac23.$$ For every fixed rational $\varepsilon$, its worst-case expected running time on strings of total length $N$ is $N^{1+o(1)}$ as $N\to\infty$ on the logarithmic-word RAM. The expectation is over internal randomness only, and the bound includes input processing, preprocessing, numerical work, random sampling and all data-structure operations. Equal strings return zero deterministically.
  - Explanation: A single randomized algorithm estimates unit-cost edit distance within a multiplicative factor with constant success probability. For each fixed accuracy it runs in almost-linear expected time on a logarithmic-word RAM, and equal strings return zero deterministically.
- **claim-connection-geometry** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-geometry)): For every interval state, $c(I,q)\ge \|z(I,q)\|$. Both $c(I,\cdot)$ and $\|z(I,\cdot)\|$ are $1$-Lipschitz in the endpoint metric. If $I$ is partitioned, in order, into $I_1,\ldots,I_m$, and $\alpha=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)$ is any list of valid child states, define $$\operatorname{conn}_r(\alpha)=\|s_1^--r^-\| +\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\|s_{i+1}^--s_i^+\|+\|s_m^+-r^+\|.$$ Then $$\begin{aligned} c(I,r)&\le\sum_i c(I_i,s_i)+\operatorname{conn}_r(\alpha),\label{eq:connection}\\ \|z(I,r)\|&\le\sum_i\|z(I_i,s_i)\|+\operatorname{conn}_r(\alpha). \label{eq:shift-connection} \end{aligned}$$ The connection inequalities also hold for finite target intervals in any extension of $y$ beyond its stored endpoints.
  - Explanation: Edit cost dominates the length imbalance, and both are Lipschitz in the endpoints. A parent's cost is bounded by the child costs plus a connection charge for gaps and overlaps between child targets.
- **claim-initial-seed** (theorem, [source](#stmt-thm-seed)): With the parameters and labeled interval tree of Section <a href="#sec:geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:geometry">2</a>, there is a lazily evaluated random table $U^{(0)}(I,q)$ of integers in $[0,N]$ such that, with probability at least $0.99$, simultaneously at every state, $$\label{eq:seed-guarantee} c(I,q)\le U^{(0)}(I,q)\le A_{\mathrm{init}}c(I,q).$$ Every zero-cost state has value zero on every execution. Conditional on any first request for an entry and the previously exposed randomness, its expected evaluation cost is at most $(1+\|I\|)2^{o(H)}$, uniformly in the state. This cost bound includes arithmetic and random sampling and does not require <a href="#eq:seed-guarantee" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:seed-guarantee">[eq:seed-guarantee]</a> to hold.
  - Explanation: A lazily evaluated random integer table gives coarse upper approximations at every interval state simultaneously with high probability. Zero-cost states always get zero, and the conditional expected cost of a first request is subpolynomial in the exponent scale.
- **claim-shift-tree-bounds** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-shift-tree)): At the root $o$, $$d\le T_o(0),\qquad T_o(0)\le(1+2BD_0)d\quad\hbox{if }k\ge d.$$
  - Explanation: The shift-tree value at the root with zero shift upper-bounds the padded distance, and is within a factor governed by branching and depth once the guess dominates the distance.
- **claim-coarse-precision** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-coarse-precision)): Except on an event of probability less than $0.01$, simultaneously for all initial entries, all guesses, all their nodes, and all shifts, $$\label{eq:coarse-accuracy} T_w(v)/f_w-a_w\le\widetilde T_w(v)\le f_wT_w(v)+a_w, \qquad f_w=\left(\frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda}\right)^{\operatorname{height}(w)} \le2.$$
  - Explanation: Precision-sampled estimates track the true shift-tree values up to a bounded multiplicative factor and an additive allowance, simultaneously over all entries, guesses, nodes and shifts, outside a small-probability event.
- **claim-refinement** (theorem, [source](#stmt-thm-refinement)): Use the parameters and interval tree of Section <a href="#sec:geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:geometry">2</a> in the large-input branch. Let $A$ be a power of two with $1\le A\le A_{\rm init}$, and let $U$ be an integer table on every labeled tree node and every valid target state, with $$0\le U(I,q)\le N,\qquad c(I,q)\le U(I,q)\le A c(I,q).$$ Set $a=\max\{1,A/F\}$. There is a randomized, finitely executable refinement table $d_S$ such that, for every state $(I,q)$, $$\label{eq:refinement-guarantee} d_S(I,q)\ge c(I,q)/a,\qquad \mathbb E\bigl[(d_S(I,q)-c(I,q))_+\bigr]\le c(I,q)/\ell.$$ The first inequality holds for every outcome of the refinement randomness; the expectation in the second is conditional on the fixed table $U$. At zero-cost states the returned value is zero for every outcome.
  - Explanation: One refinement pass lowers the seed approximation factor. It keeps a deterministic lower bound on true cost and bounds the expected positive excess by a small fraction of the true cost, conditional on the fixed good seed.
- **claim-initial-cones** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-initial-cones)): For the fixed seed in Theorem <a href="#thm:refinement" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:refinement">6</a>, $$\label{eq:initial-cones} \max\{c/a,\|z\|\}\le w_0\le2Fc, \qquad \operatorname{Lip}(w_0(I,\cdot))\le L_0.$$ At a nonleaf, the following local rule computes this global minimum exactly. If $U(I,q)=0$, return zero. Otherwise omit the zero cones, enumerate scales $$\label{eq:initial-local-scales} U(I,q)/(16A^2)\le b\le4A U(I,q),$$ and enumerate grid centers at sup distance at most $U(I,q)$ from $q$, retaining the eligibility test $b/2\le U(I,r)\le4Ab$.
  - Explanation: The lower envelope of cones is Lipschitz, stays between the scaled lower bound and a multiple of true cost, and can be computed exactly by a local enumeration of scales and grid centers.
- **claim-cone-locality** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-cone-locality)): Fix a good seed as in Theorem <a href="#thm:refinement" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:refinement">6</a>. Take a minimum of $w_0(I,q)$ and any family of cones of slope $L$ with nonnegative base costs at representatives $(b,r)$. If $w_0(I,q)=0$, its value is zero. Otherwise it suffices to enumerate scales $$\label{eq:local-scales} w_0(I,q)/(16F)\le b\le8a w_0(I,q)$$ and the following whole cells at each scale. Partition endpoint-pair space into half-open cells of side $\theta b$ on each axis, with lower boundaries at multiples of $\theta b$. Enumerate the cells intersecting the closed sup square of radius $w_0(I,q)$ about $q$, and all valid grid representatives in these cells.
  - Explanation: Minima of cone families are computed exactly by enumerating a bounded range of scales and whole cells near the query, so the local rule coincides with the global minimum.
- **claim-refinement-invariants** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-refinement-invariants)): For a seed satisfying Theorem <a href="#thm:refinement" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:refinement">6</a>, every outcome of the refinement obeys $$\begin{aligned} \max\{c/a,\|z\|\}&\le d_t\le d_{t-1}\le w_0, \label{eq:refinement-invariants}\\ d_t(I,q)&\le(1+\delta)d_t(I,q')+L\|q-q'\|_1. \label{eq:refinement-lipschitz} \end{aligned}$$ At nonleaves one also has $$\label{eq:bellman-sandwich} \mathcal B_I(d_t)(q)\le d_t(I,q) \le\mathcal B_I(d_{t-1})(q).$$ For $d_0$, the spatial bound holds with Lipschitz constant $L$ and without the factor $1+\delta$.
  - Explanation: On every outcome the refinement tables are nonincreasing in the index, bounded below by the scaled cost and the shift, Lipschitz up to a small factor, and sandwiched by Bellman updates.
- **claim-group-accuracy** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-group-accuracy)): Under the seed hypothesis of Theorem <a href="#thm:refinement" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:refinement">6</a>, fix complete child tables and one group at time $t$. With conditional probability at least $1-H^{-4}$, all action-cost estimates used to choose its representative are within $\gamma b$ of their actual costs. Consequently, for any specified unskipped member $(b,r)$ of this group, on the same event, simultaneously for every valid parent state $q$ and every $\alpha\in\mathcal C_{b,r}$, $$\label{eq:group-accuracy} \Pi_t(I,q)\le L\|q-r\|_1+(1+\delta)x_t(\alpha)+e_*b, \qquad e_*=2\gamma+512LF\theta\le\kappa\delta.$$ Here the inequality uses the global cone minimum, equivalently its local evaluation from Lemma <a href="#lem:cone-locality" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:cone-locality">8</a>.
  - Explanation: With high conditional probability the sampled group estimates are accurate, so the selected representative is nearly as good as any specified band member, with a small additive error.
- **claim-comparison-tree** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-comparison-tree)): At each nonterminal of the comparison tree, $(b,r)$ is a representative, $b$ satisfies the local scale restriction <a href="#eq:local-scales" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:local-scales">[eq:local-scales]</a>, and $\alpha^*$ is a wide action whose endpoint shifts are within $6b$ of $p_0=r^- -l$. Writing $c_i=c(I_i,q_i)$, we have $$\label{eq:comparison-split} c(I,r)\le\sum_i c_i\le (1+4M/P)c, \qquad c\le Le+\sum_i c_i.$$ Let $C_{\mathrm{term}}$ be the sum of terminal true costs. Then $$\label{eq:comparison-totals} \begin{aligned} C_{\mathrm{term}}&\le(1+8MJ/P)D\le2D,\\ \sum_{\mathrm{nonterminal}}c&\le2JD, &\sum_{\mathrm{nonterminal}}e&\le4JD/P. \end{aligned}$$ The sum of true costs at any depth is at most $2D$, also if stopped costs are carried unchanged to subsequent depths. At every terminal, $m=c$ and every refinement estimate equals $c$.
  - Explanation: The proof-only comparison tree built from optimal alignments has valid representatives and wide actions at each nonterminal, with bounded total terminal and nonterminal costs.
- **claim-curvature-telescope** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-curvature-telescope)): On the fixed comparison tree, put $h=Le+w_0(I,q)/T$ at each nonterminal. Then $$\label{eq:curvature-structural} \sum_{\mathrm{nonterminal}}(K+G) \le4C_{\mathrm{term}}+3\sum_{\mathrm{nonterminal}}e +4\sum_{\mathrm{nonterminal}}h.$$ Consequently, $$\label{eq:curvature-total} \sum_{\mathrm{nonterminal}}(K+G) \le5000F(1+J/P+J/T)D.$$
  - Explanation: Cost-weighted curvature and mass discrepancy telescope over the comparison tree, bounding their total in terms of the root cost.
- **claim-bad-node-cost** (theorem, [source](#stmt-cor-bad-node-cost)): The total true cost of bad nodes satisfies $$\label{eq:bad-node-cost} \sum_{\mathrm{bad}}c \le10000FH^{1/4}(1+J/P+J/T)D.$$
  - Explanation: Nodes with large curvature or mass gap carry only a controlled total true cost.
- **claim-comparison-band** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-comparison-band)): At a non-bad comparison node with $\|\widehat v\|\le1-\tau$, the action $\alpha^*$ belongs to $\mathcal C_{b,r}$. Its representative is not skipped: the band is nonempty, $h_\Sigma\le64Fb$, and the rounded action $\beta(b,r)$ passes both the wide-action and imbalance guards.
  - Explanation: At a node with small curvature that passes the velocity test, the comparison action lies in the computed band and the rounding guards pass, so the representative is unskipped.
- **claim-generic-regret** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-generic-regret)): At every nonterminal comparison node, $$\label{eq:generic-regret} \sum_{t=1}^S\mathcal R_t \le \sum_i\bigl(\overline d_0-\overline d_S\bigr)(I_i,q_i) \le \sum_i(m_i-\|z_i\|) \le W-\|z(I,r)\|,$$ where $z_i=z(I_i,q_i)$. In particular, the bound is at most $4Fc$. If the node is not bad and $\|\widehat v\|>1-\tau$, it is at most $(H^{-1/4}+4\tau F)c$.
  - Explanation: Summed clipped regret at any comparison node is bounded by the drop in child tables and by the mass minus the shift, which gives a small bound when the velocity is near its limit.
- **claim-entropy-regret** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-entropy)): Let $\mathcal Q$ be a nonempty compact convex set of probability vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, containing a vector with every coordinate positive. Partition the coordinates into blocks, and suppose that the total mass in each block is the same for every vector in $\mathcal Q$. For an integer $S\ge1$, let $f_0,\ldots,f_S\in[0,1]^d$ be coordinatewise nonincreasing. For $\eta>0$ and $0<\kappa<1/2$, set $$\widehat g_t=-f_{t-1},\qquad \Delta_t=f_{t-1}-f_t,\qquad u_t=\widehat g_t+(1-2\kappa)\Delta_t.$$ Suppose that the range of $\Delta_t$ within each block is at most $\kappa/\eta$ for every $1\le t\le S$. Let $\rho_t$ maximize $$\mathcal H(\rho)+ \eta\left\langle\sum_{j<t}u_j+\widehat g_t,\rho\right\rangle \quad\text{over }\rho\in\mathcal Q, \qquad \mathcal H(\rho)=-\sum_k\rho_k\ln\rho_k,$$ with $0\ln0=0$. For every $\rho^*\in\mathcal Q$ and every integer $0\le s\le S$, $$\label{eq:entropy-regret} \begin{split} \sum_{t=1}^s \left\langle f_t+\kappa\Delta_t,\rho_t\right\rangle \le {}& \sum_{t=1}^s \left\langle f_t,\rho^*\right\rangle +\frac{\ln d}{\eta}+2\kappa. \end{split}$$ For any $\zeta\ge0$, replacing each $\rho_t$ on the left by a vector within $\zeta$ in $\ell_1$ distance adds at most $s\zeta$ to the bound.
  - Explanation: Entropy-regularized optimistic prediction over probability vectors with fixed block masses has regret against any comparator bounded by a logarithmic term plus a small slack, when within-block cost variation is small.
- **claim-node-regret** (theorem, [source](#stmt-prop-node-regret)): Condition on the complete child tables at such a comparison node. Then $$\label{eq:node-regret} \begin{split} \mathbb E\left[\sum_{t=1}^S\mathcal R_t \,\middle\|\,\text{child tables}\right] \le {}&h_\Sigma\left( \frac{\ln d_{\mathcal C}}{\eta} +2\kappa+SH^{-3}\right)\\ &+2\delta c+2SH^{-4}Fc. \end{split}$$ Here $h_\Sigma\le64Fb$ and $\ln d_{\mathcal C}\le4(p_*+21)\ell$.
  - Explanation: Conditional on the child tables, the expected clipped regret at an unskipped comparison node is small, using the entropy bound before the first crossing and a charge for group failures.
- **claim-seed-amplification** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-seed-amplification)): Conditional on any fixed good preceding seed, the next seed is good for factor $4a$ except with probability at most $\exp(10H-H^2)$.
  - Explanation: Taking an order statistic over independent refinement copies makes the next seed good for the reduced factor, except with tiny probability over the whole state domain.
- **claim-finite-optimizer** (algorithm, [source](#stmt-lem-finite-optimizer)): Let $\mathcal Q$ be the convex hull of a nonempty finite list of rational probability vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, and suppose that every coordinate is positive in at least one listed vector. Given a rational vector $v$ and an integer $H\ge4$, put $G_0=H+d+2$. A rational algorithm constructs a mixture of the listed vectors whose mean $\rho$ satisfies $$\lVert\rho-\rho_t\rVert_1\le H^{-3},$$ where $\rho_t$ is the unique maximizer of $\mathcal H(\rho)+\langle v,\rho\rangle$ on $\mathcal Q$. The number of bit operations and the stored mixture size are polynomial in $G_0$, the list size, and the maximum numerator or denominator bit length of an input rational. The mixture can be sampled exactly using fair random bits, with expected cost polynomial in the same quantities and with a fixed space bound.
  - Explanation: A finite rational conditional-gradient procedure on a smoothed entropy objective yields an exactly samplable mixture of listed vectors whose mean is close to the entropy maximizer, at polynomial bit cost.
- **claim-online-local-cost** (bound, [source](#stmt-cor-online-local-cost)): For a band in the edit-distance algorithm, the numerical mixture in Section <a href="#sec:bands" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:bands">5</a> can be constructed and sampled with local expected bit cost $2^{o(H)}$, using only already gathered child values of earlier indices. The storage used by this calculation is $2^{o(H)}$ words.
  - Explanation: Constructing and sampling the numerical mixture for a band costs only subpolynomial-exponent expected bit work, using already gathered earlier child values.
- **claim-unconditional-sizes** (theorem, [source](#stmt-lem-unconditional-sizes)): On every execution, all local searches are finite. The warmup values are nonnegative integers bounded by $(2L_0+1)N$, and every refinement value satisfies $0\le d_t(I,q)\le w_0(I,q)$. Put $Q=\ell^{10}+1$, and let $h(I)$ be the remaining height of the fixed tree below $I$. Every returned $d_t(I,q)$ has denominator dividing $Q^{h(I)}$. The rational data used in band tests, group comparisons, and the numerical optimizer have bit length $H^{O(p_*+1)}$.
  - Explanation: Every local search is finite on every execution, table values stay bounded, and returned refinement values have controlled denominators and bit lengths, with no seed accuracy assumed.
- **claim-current-index-budget** (bound, [source](#stmt-lem-current-index-budget)): Evaluating one refinement entry $d_t(I,q)$ requires at most $M\ell^{O(1)}$ distinct child entries at the same pass, copy, and index $t$. This bound holds for all seeds and all sample outcomes.
  - Explanation: Shared samples and rounded actions limit the distinct same-index child entries needed per refinement entry to a factor near the branching factor.
- **claim-local-work** (bound, [source](#stmt-lem-local-work)): After collapsing the finite auxiliary calculations into table-entry evaluations, one warmup or refinement entry has at most $H^{O(p_*+1)}$ distinct inputs at earlier indices or passes. Apart from its recursive inputs, its expected bit cost is $2^{o(H)}$, uniformly conditional on the data exposed before its fresh random draws. Its local storage is at most $2^{o(H)}$ on every execution.
  - Explanation: Each warmup or refinement entry has a limited number of earlier-index inputs and subpolynomial-exponent local expected bit cost and storage.
- **claim-expected-work** (theorem, [source](#stmt-thm-work)): The large-input algorithm has worst-case expected running time $N^{1+o(1)}$ on the logarithmic-word RAM, over its internal randomness. This includes input processing, preprocessing, initial and refined table calculations, all rational arithmetic, sampling, and data-structure operations. Its workspace on every execution is bounded by a fixed polynomial in $N$. Together with the exact fallbacks, the same program has the claimed expected asymptotic bound for each fixed rational $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$.
  - Explanation: Counting dependency paths, local costs and conditional first-request costs shows the large-input algorithm has almost-linear worst-case expected running time and polynomial workspace.

```json
        "exact_quote": "Let $\\mathcal Q$ be the convex hull of a nonempty finite list of rational probability vectors in $\\mathbb R^d$, and suppose that every coordinate is positive in at least one listed vector. Given a rational vector $v$ and an integer $H\\ge4$, put $G_0=H+d+2$. A rational algorithm constructs a mixture of the listed vectors whose mean $\\rho$ satisfies $$\\lVert\\rho-\\rho_t\\rVert_1\\le H^{-3},$$ where $\\rho_t$ is the unique maximizer of $\\mathcal H(\\rho)+\\langle v,\\rho\\rangle$ on $\\mathcal Q$. The number of bit operations and the stored mixture size are polynomial in $G_0$, the list size, and the maximum numerator or denominator bit length of an input rational. <a id="pm-s2"></a>
```
## 2. Definitions, validity and bounds

- **unit-cost edit distance** ([source](#sec:intro)): The unit-cost edit distance $\operatorname{ED}(x,y)$ is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform a string $x$ into a string $y$.
- **interval state** ([source](#pm-h-10)): For an interval $I=(l,u]$ of the first string, an interval state is $(I,q)$, where $q=(q^-,q^+)$ is an integer pair with $0\le q^-\le q^+\le \|y\|$.

<a id="pm-s3"></a>
## 3. Proof roadmap

- **step-geometry** [claim](#stmt-lem-geometry) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-geometry): Walk on the target boundary, selecting forward crossings and charging backward ones to connecting jumps. -> cost and shift connection inequalities
- **step-shift-tree** [claim](#stmt-lem-shift-tree) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-shift-tree): Concatenate shifted leaf targets and use the connection inequality; compare with an optimal alignment's shifts. -> two-sided root bound for the shift tree
- **step-coarse-precision** [claim](#stmt-lem-coarse-precision) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-coarse-precision): Pathwise sandwich of thresholded contributions plus Bernstein concentration and induction from the leaves. -> accuracy of precision-sampled estimates
- **step-initial-seed** [claim](#stmt-thm-seed) / [proof](#pm-h-17): Take a minimum over guesses, clamp, and bound expected array work with private streams exposed only at first request. -> lazy initial table with conditional cost bound
- **step-initial-cones** [claim](#stmt-lem-initial-cones) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-initial-cones): Cone domination, an eligible grid center at the true-cost scale, and localization of minimizers. -> Lipschitz envelope with exact local rule
- **step-cone-locality** [claim](#stmt-lem-cone-locality) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-cone-locality): Competitive cones have nearby centers and bounded scales, so whole-cell enumeration is exact. -> local evaluation of cone minima
- **step-refinement-invariants** [claim](#stmt-lem-refinement-invariants) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-refinement-invariants): Induction on height and index using monotonicity of the Bellman operator and the clipped update. -> monotone, Lipschitz, sandwiched refinement tables
- **step-group-accuracy** [claim](#stmt-lem-group-accuracy) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-group-accuracy): Bernstein bound on shared child samples with a union bound over scales and members. -> accurate group selection
- **step-comparison-tree** [claim](#stmt-lem-comparison-tree) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-comparison-tree): Round optimal alignment anchors to the grid and track cost growth by level. -> comparison tree with cost totals
- **step-curvature-telescope** [claim](#stmt-lem-curvature-telescope) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-curvature-telescope): Averaged warmup inequalities, mass conservation and an energy telescope over the tree. -> total curvature bound
- **step-bad-node-cost** [claim](#stmt-cor-bad-node-cost) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cor-bad-node-cost): Bound each bad node's cost by its curvature and gap and sum. -> total cost of bad nodes
- **step-comparison-band** [claim](#stmt-lem-comparison-band) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-comparison-band): Weighted Cauchy-Schwarz on the shift deviations and prefix-cost bounds place the comparison action in the band. -> band coverage and guards
- **step-generic-regret** [claim](#stmt-lem-generic-regret) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-generic-regret): Telescoping of clipped values with child-wise case analysis. -> unconditional regret bound
- **step-entropy-regret** [claim](#stmt-lem-entropy) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-entropy): Potential function argument with relative-entropy penalty and an exponential estimate within blocks. -> regret bound for entropy-regularized prediction
- **step-node-regret** [claim](#stmt-prop-node-regret) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-node-regret): Split at the first crossing, apply the entropy bound before it and a group-failure charge. -> expected clipped regret at an unskipped node
- **step-refinement-accuracy** [claim](#stmt-thm-refinement) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-node-regret-2): Sum node regrets over the comparison tree by linearity of expectation across bad, high-velocity and band nodes. -> refinement guarantee
- **step-seed-amplification** [claim](#stmt-lem-seed-amplification) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-seed-amplification): Markov bound per copy, order statistic over independent copies and a union over the state domain. -> improved simultaneous seed
- **step-finite-optimizer** [claim](#stmt-lem-finite-optimizer) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-finite-optimizer): Fixed-step conditional gradient on a smoothed objective, exact mixture weights and rejection sampling. -> rational sampleable mixture near the maximizer
- **step-online-local-cost** [claim](#stmt-cor-online-local-cost) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cor-online-local-cost): Bound dimension and bit sizes of a band and apply the finite optimizer. -> subpolynomial-exponent local cost
- **step-unconditional-sizes** [claim](#stmt-lem-unconditional-sizes) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-unconditional-sizes): Induction on tree height with clamped integer seeds and denominators dividing powers of one base. -> finiteness and size bounds on every execution
- **step-current-index-budget** [claim](#stmt-lem-current-index-budget) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-current-index-budget): Count rounded states per sampled child and cancel the scale ratios. -> bound on same-index child calls
- **step-local-work** [claim](#stmt-lem-local-work) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-local-work): Enumerate wide lists, band candidates and dictionary lookups against stored inputs. -> local evaluation cost
- **step-expected-work** [claim](#stmt-thm-work) / [proof](#proof-stmt-thm-work): Count dependency paths by depth, sum local and conditional first-request costs, and bound storage. -> almost-linear expected time
- **step-main-assembly** [claim](#stmt-thm-main) / [proof](#pm-h-39): Iterate seed amplification, apply a final refinement, and combine failure probabilities with the running-time theorem. -> approximation scheme

<a id="pm-s4"></a>
## 4. Engineering Triptych

### Panel 1 - epistemic contract

- **inv-connection-inequality**: For any ordered partition of a source interval into child intervals and any list of valid child target states, the parent edit cost is at most the sum of the child costs plus the connection charge for gaps, overlaps and the two outer endpoints.

### Panel 2 - negative knowledge

- **anti-exact-distance**: Treating the connection-charge inequality as an equality, i.e. as an exact formula for the parent distance. -> The inequality is one-sided; gaps and overlaps between child targets can make the right side strictly larger than the true parent cost.
- **anti-deterministic-guarantee**: Using the full randomized scheme as a deterministic exact comparator for non-equal strings. -> The estimate is correct only with probability at least two thirds, so a wrong answer is possible on unequal inputs.

### Panel 3 - reference implementation and oracle

Applicability: `algorithmic`. The full scheme is randomized and asymptotic, so it is not tested here. The finite constructive content checked is the connection-cost computation and the connection inequality of the geometry lemma, on small explicit inputs with an exact edit-distance routine.

```python
# INPUTS: stdin with 5 lines: x; y; 'r- r+'; cut points l_0..l_m of x; child states 's1- s1+ s2- s2+ ...' ('-' denotes an empty string)
# PRECONDITIONS: cuts start at 0, are nondecreasing and end at len(x); 0<=r-<=r+<=len(y); every child state is a valid pair within y
# OUTPUTS: one line 'c sumc conn' = ED(x,y[r-:r+]), sum of child costs, connection charge
# TIME: O(|x|*|y|) per edit distance call, polynomial overall
# SPACE: O(|y|) per edit distance call
# ARITHMETIC: exact integer arithmetic
# FAILURE: malformed input raises an exception and exits non-zero
import sys

def ed(a, b):
    prev = list(range(len(b) + 1))
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        cur = [i] + [0] * len(b)
        for j in range(1, len(b) + 1):
            cur[j] = min(prev[j] + 1, cur[j-1] + 1, prev[j-1] + (a[i-1] != b[j-1]))
        prev = cur
    return prev[-1]

lines = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
x = lines[0].strip()
y = lines[1].strip()
x = '' if x == '-' else x
y = '' if y == '-' else y
r0, r1 = [int(t) for t in lines[2].split()]
cuts = [int(t) for t in lines[3].split()]
flat = [int(t) for t in lines[4].split()]
m = len(cuts) - 1
s = [(flat[2*i], flat[2*i+1]) for i in range(m)]
c = ed(x, y[r0:r1])
sumc = sum(ed(x[cuts[i]:cuts[i+1]], y[s[i][0]:s[i][1]]) for i in range(m))
conn = abs(s[0][0]-r0) + sum(abs(s[i+1][0]-s[i][1]) for i in range(m-1)) + abs(s[-1][1]-r1)
print(c, sumc, conn)
```

<a id="pm-s6"></a>
## 6. Applicability limits and search

- **limit-fixed-accuracy-only** (hypothesis): The almost-linear running time is asserted pointwise for each fixed rational accuracy. No bound that is polynomial in the inverse accuracy, and no joint bound when the accuracy varies with the input length, is claimed. Blocked use: ['Choosing the accuracy as a function of N and quoting the almost-linear time bound', 'Quoting a cost that is polynomial in 1/epsilon']
- **limit-exact-fallback-thresholds** (edge_case): Below accuracy-dependent thresholds the algorithm switches to exact quadratic dynamic programming. The approximation scheme itself runs only in the large-input branch, for inputs beyond these very large cutoffs. Blocked use: ['Expecting subquadratic behaviour on moderate input sizes', 'Benchmarking the approximate branch on small or medium strings']
- **limit-estimate-only-output** (formal_scope): The output is a single distance estimate. No alignment or edit script is produced, so any task that needs the edit operations themselves is outside the result. Blocked use: ['Generating diffs or patches from the output', 'Recovering an optimal alignment from the algorithm']
- **limit-unit-cost-model** (hypothesis): All three edit operations have cost one. Weighted costs, affine gaps and substitution matrices are not covered by the guarantee. Blocked use: ['Applying the scheme to weighted or affine-gap sequence alignment']
- **limit-randomized-guarantee** (edge_case): Only the equal-strings case is answered deterministically. On other inputs the estimate is correct only with constant probability, and the lower bound is not asserted on executions with a bad seed. Blocked use: ['Using the estimate as an exact or zero-error comparator on unequal strings', 'Assuming the lower bound holds on every execution']
- **limit-expectation-over-internal-randomness** (approximation): The time bound is an expectation over internal randomness only, in the worst case over inputs, on the logarithmic-word RAM. It is not a high-probability or deterministic worst-case time bound. Blocked use: ['Claiming a hard real-time deadline from the expected-time bound', 'Transferring the bound to other machine models without re-analysis']
- **limit-work-bounds-without-accuracy-events** (formal_scope): The recursive-request and cost bounds hold on every execution, including inaccurate seeds. The accuracy invariants hold only under a good seed, so cost and correctness must not be conflated. Blocked use: ['Assuming correctness invariants on executions with an inaccurate seed']
- **limit-comparison-tree-analysis-only** (nonconstructive): The comparison tree built from optimal alignments is an analysis device. The algorithm never computes it, so it cannot serve as a data structure or a source of an alignment. Blocked use: ['Implementing the comparison tree as part of the algorithm', 'Using it to extract an optimal alignment']

<a id="pm-formal"></a>
### Formal statement (Lean 4)

Corpus status: formalized in the source corpus (toolchain `leanprover/lean4:v4.34.1`, Mathlib `d13f23b723b8a846827a245b89c10fc7d3f11612`). Not re-checked here; the statements give the exact quantifiers and hypotheses, not a proof.

Scope note of family 121 (`lean/docs/121.md`, verbatim):

> The following describes the scope of the Lean formalization related to the following accompanying paper(s):
>
> - [An Almost-Linear Approximation Scheme for Edit Distance](../../preprints/An-Almost-Linear-Approximation-Scheme-for-Edit-Distance-September-24-2026/paper.pdf)
>
> ## Scope
>
> The formalization gives a randomized $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for unit-cost edit distance between explicitly stored integer strings, for every fixed rational $0<\varepsilon<1$. Its estimate is at least the true distance and at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times it with probability at least $2/3$; equal strings return zero on every execution.
>
> For total length at most $N$ and integer symbols bounded by a fixed polynomial in $N$, expected work is at most $(N+2)^{1+\eta}$ for every fixed $\eta>0$ and all sufficiently large $N$. Space is polynomially bounded on every execution.

```lean
def value {ι : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (oracle : ι → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction) : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β → β
  | .done result => result
  | .read key next => value oracle (next (oracle key))
  | .charge _ next => value oracle next
```

```lean
def work {ι : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (oracle : ι → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction) (readWork : ι → ℕ) : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β → ℕ
  | .done _ => 0
  | .read key next => readWork key + work oracle readWork (next (oracle key))
  | .charge steps next => steps + work oracle readWork next
```

```lean
def bind {ι : Type u_1} {α : Type u_2} {β : Type u_3} : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι α → (α → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β) → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β
  | .done result, next => next result
  | .read key continuation, next => .read key (fun word => bind (continuation word) next)
  | .charge steps continuation, next => .charge steps (bind continuation next)
```

```lean
def compute {ι : Type u_1} {α : Type u_2} (execution : α × ℕ) : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι α
```

```lean
def mapKeysWithWork {ι : Type u_1} {κ : Type u_2} {β : Type u_3} (f : ι → κ × ℕ) : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery κ β
  | .done result => .done result
  | .read key next => .charge (f key).2
      (.read (f key).1 (fun word => mapKeysWithWork f (next word)))
  | .charge steps next => .charge steps (mapKeysWithWork f next)
```

```lean
def restrictWithWork {ι : Type u_1} (P : ι → Prop)
    (test : ι → Bool × ℕ) (htest : ∀ key, (test key).1 = true ↔ P key) :
    OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery {key // P key} OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction
  | .done result => .done result
  | .charge steps next => .charge steps (restrictWithWork P test htest next)
  | .read key next => .charge (test key).2
      (if h : (test key).1 = true then
        .read ⟨key, (htest key).mp h⟩ (fun word => restrictWithWork P test htest (next word))
       else restrictWithWork P test htest (next (OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction.nat 0)))
```

```lean
def runMemo {ι : Type u_1} {κ : Type u_2}
    (ask : ι → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → OAI.EditApproximation.BitRecursiveMemoResult κ) :
    OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → OAI.EditApproximation.BitRecursiveMemoResult κ
  | .done result, memory => ⟨result, memory, [], 0, 0, 0⟩
  | .read key next, memory =>
    let first
```

```lean
inductive Footprint {ι : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β → Type _ where
  | done (value : β) : Footprint (.done value)
  | read (key : ι) (next : OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β)
      (continuation : ∀ word, Footprint (next word)) : Footprint (.read key next)
  | charge {steps : ℕ} {next : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β} (cells : ℕ)
      (continuation : Footprint next) : Footprint (.charge steps next)
```

```lean
def collect {ι : Type u_1} {κ : Type u_2} {β : Type u_3} (reader : κ → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction) :
    List κ → (List OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β) → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β
  | [], next => next []
  | key :: rest, next => (reader key).bind (fun word =>
      .charge 3 (collect reader rest (fun words => next (word :: words))))
```

```lean
def scoredArgmaxAllocation {α : Type u_1} (score : α → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction × ℕ)
    (allocation : α → ℕ) : List α → ℕ
  | [] => 0
  | a :: rest =>
    scoredArgmaxAllocation score allocation rest + allocation a +
      match (OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction.scoredArgmaxWithWork score rest).1 with
      | none => 1
      | some best => OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction.ltAllocation (score a).1 best.2 + 1
```

```lean
def run {ι : Type u_1} {κ : Type u_2} (ask : ι → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo ℚ → OAI.EditApproximation.RecursiveMemoResult κ) :
    OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo ℚ → OAI.EditApproximation.RecursiveMemoResult κ
  | .done result, memory => ⟨result, memory, [], 0, 0⟩
  | .read key next, memory =>
    let first
```

```lean
def bind {ι : Type u_1} : OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι → (ℚ → OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι) → OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι
  | .done result, next => next result
  | .read key continuation, next => .read key (fun result => bind (continuation result) next)
```

```lean
def mapKeys {ι : Type u_1} {κ : Type u_2} (f : ι → κ) : OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι → OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery κ
  | .done result => .done result
  | .read key next => .read (f key) (fun answer => mapKeys f (next answer))
```

```lean
def restrict {ι : Type u_1} (P : ι → Prop) [DecidablePred P] : OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι → OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery {key // P key}
  | .done result => .done result
  | .read key next => if h : P key then
      .read ⟨key, h⟩ (fun answer => restrict P (next answer))
    else restrict P (next 0)
```

```lean
def requestWork {ι : Type u_1} {κ : Type u_2} (ask : ι → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo ℚ → OAI.EditApproximation.RecursiveMemoResult κ)
    (cost : ι → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo ℚ → ℕ) : OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo ℚ → ℕ
  | .done _, _ => 0
  | .read key next, memory =>
      let first
```

```lean
def collect {ι : Type u_1} {κ : Type u_2} (reader : κ → OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι) :
    List κ → (List ℚ → OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι) → OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery ι
  | [], next => next []
  | key :: keys, next => OAI.EditApproximation.FiniteQuery.bind (reader key) fun result =>
      collect reader keys (fun results => next (result :: results))
```

```lean
    (D : ℕ) → List α → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D
  | 0, source => .leaf source.head?
  | D + 1, source => .branch (fun i =>
      coarseSourceTreeOfList B D ((source.drop (i.val * B ^ D)).take (B ^ D)))
```

```lean
def count : OAI.EditApproximation.PositionCounts → ℕ
  | .empty => 0
  | .node n _ _ => n
```

```lean
def left : OAI.EditApproximation.PositionCounts → OAI.EditApproximation.PositionCounts
  | .empty => .empty
  | .node _ l _ => l
```

```lean
def right : OAI.EditApproximation.PositionCounts → OAI.EditApproximation.PositionCounts
  | .empty => .empty
  | .node _ _ r => r
```

```lean
def storageBits : OAI.EditApproximation.PositionCounts → ℕ
  | .empty => 0
  | .node n l r => Nat.size n + 3 + l.storageBits + r.storageBits
```

```lean
def add (tree : OAI.EditApproximation.PositionCounts) : ℕ → ℕ → OAI.EditApproximation.PositionCounts
  | 0, _ => .node (tree.count + 1) tree.left tree.right
  | d + 1, i =>
    if i < 2 ^ d then
      .node (tree.count + 1) (tree.left.add d i) tree.right
    else .node (tree.count + 1) tree.left (tree.right.add d (i - 2 ^ d))
```

```lean
def collect {ι : Type u_1} {κ : Type u_2} {β : Type u_3} (reader : κ → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction)
    (allocation : ∀ key, OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery.Footprint (reader key)) :
    (inputs : List κ) → (next : List OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β) →
      (∀ words, OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery.Footprint (next words)) → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery.Footprint (OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery.collect reader inputs next)
  | [], _, continuation => continuation []
  | key :: rest, next, continuation =>
    (allocation key).bind _ fun word => .charge 1
      (collect reader allocation rest (fun words => next (word :: words))
        (fun words => continuation (word :: words)))
```

```lean
structure UnskippedBand {α : Type u_1} (source target : List α) {M : ℕ}
    (parent : OAI.EditApproximation.TargetInterval source.length) (b P thetaExponent : ℕ)
    (tau F : ℚ) (child initial : Fin M → OAI.EditApproximation.TargetInterval target.length → ℚ) where
  center : OAI.EditApproximation.TargetInterval target.length
  nonempty : OAI.EditApproximation.representativeBandActions source target parent center b P tau
    ((2 : ℚ) ^ (-(thetaExponent : ℤ))) child ≠ []
  sum_guard : (∑ i, OAI.EditApproximation.bandChildEnvelope b (OAI.EditApproximation.representativeBandActions source target parent center b P tau
    ((2 : ℚ) ^ (-(thetaExponent : ℤ))) child) initial i) ≤ 64 * F * b
  wide_guard : OAI.EditApproximation.canonicalRoundedBandAction thetaExponent b
    (OAI.EditApproximation.representativeBandActions source target parent center b P tau
      ((2 : ℚ) ^ (-(thetaExponent : ℤ))) child) nonempty initial ∈ OAI.EditApproximation.wideActionList M parent center b P
  imbalance_guard : ∀ i, |rationalStateGap
    (OAI.EditApproximation.substring source (OAI.EditApproximation.sourceChild parent i).lo (OAI.EditApproximation.sourceChild parent i).hi) target
    (OAI.EditApproximation.canonicalRoundedBandAction thetaExponent b
      (OAI.EditApproximation.representativeBandActions source target parent center b P tau
        ((2 : ℚ) ^ (-(thetaExponent : ℤ))) child) nonempty initial i)| ≤
      2 * OAI.EditApproximation.bandChildEnvelope b (OAI.EditApproximation.representativeBandActions source target parent center b P tau
        ((2 : ℚ) ^ (-(thetaExponent : ℤ))) child) initial i
```

```lean
def lookup (tree : OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo α) : List Bool → Option α
  | [] => tree.value
  | false :: rest => tree.left.lookup rest
  | true :: rest => tree.right.lookup rest
```

```lean
def insert (tree : OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo α) : List Bool → α → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo α
  | [], a => .node (some a) tree.left tree.right
  | false :: rest, a => .node tree.value (tree.left.insert rest a) tree.right
  | true :: rest, a => .node tree.value tree.left (tree.right.insert rest a)
```

```lean
def coarseActiveChildrenWork {B D : ℕ} {α : Type u}
    (Q lam allowance : ℚ)
    (work : OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseThresholdDraws B D → ℚ → ℕ) :
    List (OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D × Fin B × OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseThresholdDraws B D) → ℕ

      coarseActiveChildrenWork Q lam allowance work rest
```

```lean
def fractionStorage : OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → ℕ
  | .empty => 0
  | .node value left right =>
    3 + (value.map fun word => word.numerator.bits.length + word.denominator.length + 1).getD 0 +
      left.fractionStorage + right.fractionStorage
```

```lean
def valueStorage {α : Type u_1} (bits : α → ℕ) : OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryMemo α → ℕ
  | .empty => 0
  | .node value l r => 3 + (value.map bits).getD 0 + valueStorage bits l + valueStorage bits r
```

```lean
inductive Step (substitutions : Bool) {Alpha : Type u} : List Alpha → List Alpha → Prop
  | insert (p q : List Alpha) (a : Alpha) : Step substitutions (p ++ q) (p ++ a :: q)
  | delete (p q : List Alpha) (a : Alpha) : Step substitutions (p ++ a :: q) (p ++ q)
  | substitute (h : substitutions = true) (p q : List Alpha) (a b : Alpha) :
      Step substitutions (p ++ a :: q) (p ++ b :: q)
```

```lean
inductive Script (substitutions : Bool) {Alpha : Type u} : ℕ → List Alpha → List Alpha → Prop
  | nil (x : List Alpha) : Script substitutions 0 x x
  | cons {n : ℕ} {x y z : List Alpha} (first : OAI.EditDistortion.Step substitutions x y)
      (rest : Script substitutions n y z) : Script substitutions (n + 1) x z
```

```lean
def word {B : ℕ} {α : Type u} : {D : ℕ} → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D → List α
  | _, .leaf letter => letter.toList
  | _, .branch children => (List.ofFn fun i => word (children i)).flatten
```

```lean
def coarseLabelCount {B : ℕ} {α : Type u_1} (Q lam : ℚ) :
    {d : ℕ} → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α d → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseThresholdDraws B d → ℚ → ℕ
  | _, tree, draws, allowance =>
    if (tree.word.length : ℚ) ≤ allowance then 0 else
    match tree, draws with
    | .leaf _, _ => 0
    | .branch children, (draws, below) => B +
      OAI.EditApproximation.coarseLabelChildren Q lam allowance (fun child => coarseLabelCount Q lam child)
        (List.ofFn fun i => (children i, draws i, below i))
```

```lean
    (value : OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D → ℕ → Fin (2 * k + 1) → ℕ) :
    List (OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D) → ℕ → Fin (2 * k + 1) → ℕ
  | [], _, _ => 0
  | child :: rest, start, shift =>
    univ.inf' univ_nonempty (fun next => value child start next + 2 * Nat.dist shift.val next.val) +
      coarseChildrenCost k value rest (start + child.word.length) shift
```

```lean
def coarseShiftCost {B : ℕ} {α : Type u} [DecidableEq α] (k : ℕ) (frame : List (Option α)) :
    {D : ℕ} → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D → ℕ → Fin (2 * k + 1) → ℕ
  | _, .leaf none, _, _ => 0
  | _, .leaf (some letter), start, shift =>
    if (frame[start + shift.val]?.getD none) = some letter then 0 else 1
  | _, .branch children, start, shift =>
    OAI.EditApproximation.coarseChildrenCost k (fun child => coarseShiftCost k frame child)
      (List.ofFn children) start shift
```

```lean
def coarseActiveArrayWork {B : ℕ} {α : Type u} (k : ℕ) (Q lam : ℚ) :
    {D : ℕ} → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseThresholdDraws B D → ℚ → ℕ
  | _, tree, draws, allowance =>
    if (tree.word.length : ℚ) ≤ allowance then 0 else
    match tree, draws with
    | .leaf _, _ => B * (2 * k + 1)
    | .branch children, (draws, below) =>
      B * (2 * k + 1) +
        OAI.EditApproximation.coarseActiveChildrenWork Q lam allowance (fun child => coarseActiveArrayWork k Q lam child)
          (List.ofFn fun i => (children i, draws i, below i))
```

```lean
theorem almostLinearEditDistanceRawBand (epsilon : OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction)
    (hepsilon : 0 < epsilon.value) (_hepsilonOne : epsilon.value < 1)
    :
    (∀ (source target : List ℤ) (N : ℕ), source.length + target.length ≤ N →
      (2 / 3 : ℝ) ≤ (OAI.EditApproximation.computedFullLaw (source.map OAI.EditApproximation.integerSymbolCode) (target.map OAI.EditApproximation.integerSymbolCode) N epsilon).real
        {outcome | EditDistortion.edit source target ≤ OAI.EditApproximation.integerBinaryAnswerRawBand source target N epsilon outcome ∧
          (OAI.EditApproximation.integerBinaryAnswerRawBand source target N epsilon outcome : ℝ) ≤
            (1 + (epsilon.value : ℝ)) * OAI.EditDistortion.edit source target}) ∧
    (∀ (source target : List ℤ) (N : ℕ), source = target → ∀ outcome,
      OAI.EditApproximation.integerBinaryAnswerRawBand source target N epsilon outcome = 0) ∧
    (∀ (C : ℕ) (eta : ℝ), 0 < eta → ∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop,
      ∀ source target : List ℤ, source.length + target.length ≤ N →
        (∀ z ∈ source ++ target, z.natAbs ≤ (N + 2) ^ C) →
        (∫ outcome, OAI.EditApproximation.integerBinaryWorkRawBand source target N epsilon outcome
          ∂OAI.EditApproximation.computedFullLaw (source.map OAI.EditApproximation.integerSymbolCode) (target.map OAI.EditApproximation.integerSymbolCode) N epsilon) ≤
            (N + 2 : ℝ) ^ (1 + eta)) ∧
    (∀ C : ℕ, ∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop, ∀ source target : List ℤ,
      source.length + target.length ≤ N →
        (∀ z ∈ source ++ target, z.natAbs ≤ (N + 2) ^ C) →
        ∀ outcome, OAI.EditApproximation.integerBinarySpaceFootprintRawBand source target N epsilon outcome ≤ (N + 2) ^ (C + 65564))
```

```json
      "statement_lean": "def value {ι : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (oracle : ι → OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction) : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β → β\n  | .done result => result\n  | .read key next => value oracle (next (oracle key))\n  | .charge _ next => value oracle next"

      "name": "work",

    },
    {
      "docstring": null,
      "kind": "def",
      "name": "bind",
      "statement_lean": "def bind {ι : Type u_1} {α : Type u_2} {β : Type u_3} : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι α → (α → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β) → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β\n  | .done result, next => next result\n  | .read key continuation, next => .read key (fun word => bind (continuation word) next)\n  | .charge steps continuation, next => .charge steps (bind continuation next)"
    },
    {
      "docstring": null,

      "name": "mapKeysWithWork",
      "statement_lean": "def mapKeysWithWork {ι : Type u_1} {κ : Type u_2} {β : Type u_3} (f : ι → κ × ℕ) : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery κ β\n  | .done result => .done result\n  | .read key next => .charge (f key).2\n      (.read (f key).1 (fun word => mapKeysWithWork f (next word)))\n  | .charge steps next => .charge steps (mapKeysWithWork f next)"
    },
    {
      "docstring": null,
      "kind": "def",
      "name": "restrictWithWork",
      "statement_lean": "def restrictWithWork {ι : Type u_1} (P : ι → Prop)\n    (test : ι → Bool × ℕ) (htest : ∀ key, (test key).1 = true ↔ P key) :\n    OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery {key // P key} OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction\n  | .done result => .done result\n  | .charge steps next => .charge steps (restrictWithWork P test htest next)\n  | .read key next => .charge (test key).2\n      (if h : (test key).1 = true then\n        .read ⟨key, (htest key).mp h⟩ (fun word => restrictWithWork P test htest (next word))\n       else restrictWithWork P test htest (next (OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction.nat 0)))"

      "statement_lean": "inductive Footprint {ι : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β → Type _ where\n  | done (value : β) : Footprint (.done value)\n  | read (key : ι) (next : OAI.EditApproximation.BinaryFraction → OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β)\n      (continuation : ∀ word, Footprint (next word)) : Footprint (.read key next)\n  | charge {steps : ℕ} {next : OAI.EditApproximation.BitQuery ι β} (cells : ℕ)\n      (continuation : Footprint next) : Footprint (.charge steps next)"

      "name": "coarseLabelCount",
      "statement_lean": "def coarseLabelCount {B : ℕ} {α : Type u_1} (Q lam : ℚ) :\n    {d : ℕ} → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α d → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseThresholdDraws B d → ℚ → ℕ\n  | _, tree, draws, allowance =>\n    if (tree.word.length : ℚ) ≤ allowance then 0 else\n    match tree, draws with\n    | .leaf _, _ => 0\n    | .branch children, (draws, below) => B +\n      OAI.EditApproximation.coarseLabelChildren Q lam allowance (fun child => coarseLabelCount Q lam child)\n        (List.ofFn fun i => (children i, draws i, below i))"

      "kind": "def",
      "name": "coarseChildrenCost",
      "statement_lean": "def coarseChildrenCost {B D : ℕ} {α : Type u} (k : ℕ)\n    (value : OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D → ℕ → Fin (2 * k + 1) → ℕ) :\n    List (OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D) → ℕ → Fin (2 * k + 1) → ℕ\n  | [], _, _ => 0\n  | child :: rest, start, shift =>\n    univ.inf' univ_nonempty (fun next => value child start next + 2 * Nat.dist shift.val next.val) +\n      coarseChildrenCost k value rest (start + child.word.length) shift"
    },
    {

      "name": "coarseShiftCost",
      "statement_lean": "def coarseShiftCost {B : ℕ} {α : Type u} [DecidableEq α] (k : ℕ) (frame : List (Option α)) :\n    {D : ℕ} → OAI.EditApproximation.CoarseSourceTree B α D → ℕ → Fin (2 * k + 1) → ℕ\n  | _, .leaf none, _, _ => 0\n  | _, .leaf (some letter), start, shift =>\n    if (frame[start + shift.val]?.getD none) = some letter then 0 else 1\n  | _, .branch children, start, shift =>\n    OAI.EditApproximation.coarseChildrenCost k (fun child => coarseShiftCost k frame child)\n      (List.ofFn children) start shift"
```

<a id="pm-s7"></a>
## 7. Complete mathematical paper


We give a uniform randomized approximation scheme for unit-cost edit distance. For every fixed rational $`\varepsilon\in(0,1)`$, it estimates the distance between arbitrary explicitly stored strings of total length <i>N</i> within a factor $`1+\varepsilon`$ with probability at least 2/3, in worst-case expected time $`N^{1+o(1)}`$ on a logarithmic-word RAM. The algorithm supports polynomially bounded integer alphabets and returns zero deterministically on equal strings.

<a id="sec:intro"></a>
### Introduction

The unit-cost edit distance $\operatorname{ED}(x,y)$ is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform a string $x$ into a string $y$. All three operations have cost one. The strings are stored explicitly; write $N=|x|+|y|$. Their symbols are integer labels of polynomial magnitude in $N+2$, stored in words of $O(\log(N+2))$ bits. There is no bound on the alphabet size independent of $N$.

An approximation scheme receives a rational $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and estimates the distance multiplicatively. Its guarantee must therefore include returning zero when the two strings are equal. We prove the following result.

<a id="stmt-thm-main"></a>
<div id="thm:main" class="theorem">

**Theorem 1**. *There is one uniform randomized algorithm that, given $x,y$ and a rational $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, returns a nonnegative integer $\widehat D$ such that $$\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\le \widehat D\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]
 \ge \frac23.$$ For every fixed rational $\varepsilon$, its worst-case expected running time on strings of total length $N$ is $N^{1+o(1)}$ as $N\to\infty$ on the logarithmic-word RAM. The expectation is over internal randomness only, and the bound includes input processing, preprocessing, numerical work, random sampling and all data-structure operations. Equal strings return zero deterministically.*

</div>

The program is uniform in the accuracy input. The asymptotic assertion is pointwise in each fixed rational accuracy: its constants and the threshold at which the bound applies may depend on $\varepsilon$. We do not assert polynomial dependence on $1/\varepsilon$ or a joint bound when the accuracy varies with $N$. The output is a distance estimate; no edit-script reconstruction is needed.

The algorithm uses exact computation below an accuracy-dependent input-length threshold. Section <a href="#sec:geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:geometry">2</a> gives the finite input convention and fallback rules; their thresholds are very large, so the result is an asymptotic approximation scheme.

<a id="pm-h-3"></a>
#### Context and approach

Edit distance originates in the study of errors in transmitted strings, including Levenshtein’s binary codes for insertions, deletions and bit flips (Levenshtein 1966) <a id="pm-cite-1"></a>[[Levenshtein1966](#ref-Levenshtein1966)]. The dynamic program of Wagner and Fischer (Wagner and Fischer 1974) <a id="pm-cite-2"></a>[[WagnerFischer1974](#ref-WagnerFischer1974)] computes the minimum cost of insertions, deletions and substitutions in quadratic time. Masek and Paterson (Masek and Paterson 1980) <a id="pm-cite-3"></a>[[MasekPaterson1980](#ref-MasekPaterson1980)] applied block tabulation to obtain a logarithmic speedup for fixed alphabets and suitable fixed costs. Distance-sensitive exact algorithms offer another route when few edits are needed: Ukkonen (Ukkonen 1985) <a id="pm-cite-4"></a>[[Ukkonen1985](#ref-Ukkonen1985)] developed bounded-distance methods, and Landau and Vishkin (Landau and Vishkin 1988, 1989) <a id="pm-cite-5"></a>[[LandauVishkin1988](#ref-LandauVishkin1988), [LandauVishkin1989](#ref-LandauVishkin1989)] combined furthest-reaching states with fast matching queries. Myers’s related difference algorithm (Myers 1986) <a id="pm-cite-6"></a>[[Myers1986](#ref-Myers1986)] treats insertion–deletion scripts. For unrestricted exact computation, Backurs and Indyk (Backurs and Indyk 2018) <a id="pm-cite-7"></a>[[BackursIndyk2018](#ref-BackursIndyk2018)] showed that a strongly subquadratic deterministic algorithm would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. That lower bound does not rule out fixed-factor approximation.

Approximation algorithms progressively improved the accuracy available with substantially less work. In the following historical comparisons, write $n$ for a common upper bound on the string lengths. Batu and coauthors (Batu et al. 2003) <a id="pm-cite-8"></a>[[BatuEtAl2003](#ref-BatuEtAl2003)] gave sublinear tests for fixed alphabets that distinguish sufficiently small distance from linear distance. For general pairs, Bar-Yossef, Jayram, Krauthgamer and Kumar (Bar-Yossef et al. 2004) <a id="pm-cite-9"></a>[[BarYossefEtAl2004](#ref-BarYossefEtAl2004)] obtained an $n^{3/7}$ approximation in quasi-linear time; Batu, Ergün and Sahinalp (Batu, Ergün, and Sahinalp 2006) <a id="pm-cite-10"></a>[[BatuErgunSahinalp2006](#ref-BatuErgunSahinalp2006)] improved the factor to $n^{1/3+o(1)}$. For binary strings, Ostrovsky and Rabani (Ostrovsky and Rabani 2007) <a id="pm-cite-11"></a>[[OstrovskyRabani2007](#ref-OstrovskyRabani2007)] constructed a low-distortion embedding into $\ell_1$, and Andoni and Onak (Andoni and Onak 2012) <a id="pm-cite-12"></a>[[AndoniOnak2012](#ref-AndoniOnak2012)] obtained an efficiently computable $2^{\widetilde O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ approximation in $n^{1+o(1)}$ time. Andoni, Krauthgamer and Onak (Andoni, Krauthgamer, and Onak 2010) <a id="pm-cite-13"></a>[[AndoniKrauthgamerOnak2010](#ref-AndoniKrauthgamerOnak2010)] then achieved a $(\log n)^{O(1/\xi)}$ factor in $n^{1+\xi}$ time for each fixed $\xi>0$, using a hierarchical alignment representation and nonuniformly allocated precisions.

The next advances reached constant factors. Chakraborty, Das, Goldenberg, Koucký and Saks (Chakraborty et al. 2020) <a id="pm-cite-14"></a>[[ChakrabortyEtAl2020](#ref-ChakrabortyEtAl2020)] gave a constant-factor approximation in $\widetilde O(n^{12/7})$ time. Brakensiek and Rubinstein (Brakensiek and Rubinstein 2020) <a id="pm-cite-15"></a>[[BrakensiekRubinstein2020](#ref-BrakensiekRubinstein2020)] and Koucký and Saks (Koucký and Saks 2020) <a id="pm-cite-16"></a>[[KouckySaks2020](#ref-KouckySaks2020)] independently obtained near-linear exponents for sufficiently far input pairs, with a material additive error on general pairs. Andoni and Nosatzki (Andoni and Nosatzki 2020) <a id="pm-cite-17"></a>[[AndoniNosatzki2020](#ref-AndoniNosatzki2020)] removed that restriction: for every fixed $\xi>0$, their algorithm gives an approximation factor depending only on $\xi$ in $O(n^{1+\xi})$ time. The factor depends on the exponent parameter; this is not an approximation scheme with error tending to zero. For accuracy arbitrarily close to one, Mao and Rubinstein (Mao and Rubinstein 2026, Theorem 6.1) <a id="pm-cite-18"></a>[[MaoRubinstein2026](#ref-MaoRubinstein2026)] recently obtained a randomized $(1+\varepsilon)$ approximation in $n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}$ time for every fixed positive $\varepsilon$.

The issue addressed here is how to retain fixed $(1+\varepsilon)$ accuracy while reducing the expected total work to $N^{1+o(1)}$. Recursive interval decompositions, economical evaluation of local distances, and accounting along an optimal alignment have substantial precedent in the algorithms above. In our refinement, unrestricted recursive evaluation of child distances would consume the available time even if the resulting numerical error were small. We therefore need both a narrow family that contains a suitable comparison alignment and a bound on the number of child distances actually evaluated.

For the initial estimates we adapt the shift tree and precision sampling of Andoni, Krauthgamer and Onak (Andoni, Krauthgamer, and Onak 2010, 2011) <a id="pm-cite-19"></a>[[AndoniKrauthgamerOnak2010](#ref-AndoniKrauthgamerOnak2010), [AndoniKrauthgamerOnak2011](#ref-AndoniKrauthgamerOnak2011)]. The refinement is related to Mao and Rubinstein’s use of multiscale deviation to constrain alignment paths before sampling (Mao and Rubinstein 2026) <a id="pm-cite-20"></a>[[MaoRubinstein2026](#ref-MaoRubinstein2026)]. Here we measure the alignment’s changes in relative position using preliminary cost estimates as weights. A telescoping bound on their variation controls the total cost of places where the prediction fails. An entropy-regularized prediction rule, within the framework of Rakhlin and Sridharan (Rakhlin and Sridharan 2013) <a id="pm-cite-21"></a>[[RakhlinSridharan2013](#ref-RakhlinSridharan2013)], then controls the accumulated error where the predictions can be used. We implement its optimization by a finite Frank–Wolfe procedure (Frank and Wolfe 1956; Jaggi 2013) <a id="pm-cite-22"></a>[[FrankWolfe1956](#ref-FrankWolfe1956), [Jaggi2013](#ref-Jaggi2013)]. The specialized geometric, probabilistic and numerical guarantees are proved in this paper.

Two related comparisons concern different requirements on the output or the edit costs. A single $\ell_1$ embedding of all binary strings up to a length bound must incur growing distortion (OpenAI 2026, Theorem 1.1) <a id="pm-cite-23"></a>[[OpenAIEditDistortion2026](#ref-OpenAIEditDistortion2026)]. Our algorithm estimates the distance of the supplied pair and does not construct such a common embedding. Recent algorithms for metric-weighted edit costs obtain $(3+\varepsilon)$ approximation in strongly subquadratic time (Mader, Tavasoli, and Wang 2026; Das, Kipouridis, and Kociumaka 2026) <a id="pm-cite-24"></a>[[MaderTavasoliWang2026](#ref-MaderTavasoliWang2026), [DasKipouridisKociumaka2026](#ref-DasKipouridisKociumaka2026)]; their cost model is broader than the unit-cost model treated here.

<a id="pm-h-4"></a>
#### Proof overview

Recursively partition the first string into a tree of intervals, ending at intervals of length at most one. An interval state consists of a source interval $I$ and a target interval in the second string; its true cost is the edit distance between the two substrings. An action at a nonleaf assigns one target interval to each source child. We charge the sum of the child estimates together with penalties for gaps or overlaps between successive target endpoints and at the two outer endpoints. These penalties let us compare nearby actions without requiring their target intervals to join exactly.

<a id="pm-h-5"></a>
###### Estimates that can be requested adaptively.

The initial seed is an integer table whose entries give coarse upper approximations to all interval-state costs. Although the algorithm evaluates only requested entries, the accuracy event covers the entire domain: later queries may depend on earlier random answers. Each initial entry uses a private random stream, so its expected evaluation cost can also be bounded conditional on the request that first exposes it. Accuracy and expected work thus use different probability statements. Successive refinement passes improve the seed approximation factor.

<a id="pm-h-6"></a>
###### Predicting where an alignment goes.

One refinement starts from such a seed. It first propagates estimates through a wide family of actions and averages the resulting preliminary tables to obtain cost proxies. At a source cut, the alignment’s shift is the target position minus the source position. The total shift change divided by the predicted total cost suggests how this shift should evolve as prefix cost accumulates. Requiring agreement with that prediction restricts the possible target positions at each cut to a narrow band. The algorithm computes these bands from the cost proxies alone.

To analyze them, fix optimal alignments and recursively round their child endpoints. This gives a comparison tree that the algorithm never computes. A cost-weighted variance measures how far the comparison shifts depart from the predicted evolution. Its sum telescopes, with additional charges for disagreements among the cost proxies. Consequently the total cost of nodes with large discrepancies is controlled. At the other nodes, either the substring-length difference already accounts for almost all predicted cost, giving a direct error bound, or the computed band contains the comparison action.

<a id="pm-h-7"></a>
###### From a band to a better seed.

Within a band, an entropy-regularized rule predicts an action using earlier child values. Shared samples also compare rounded actions across nearby representatives. The resulting estimates decrease with the refinement index. After conditioning on complete child tables, the parent samples retain their prescribed laws, and an online inequality bounds cumulative excess over the comparison action. Some intermediate estimates can be smaller than true cost. The analysis therefore clips them from below at true cost, so an underestimate at one node cannot cancel an error elsewhere. Summing over the comparison tree gives a small expected positive error at any fixed queried state, together with a deterministic multiplicative lower bound. Independent repetitions, rescaling and medians turn these two bounds into a simultaneous one-sided seed with a smaller approximation factor. Repeating this improvement and making one final refinement gives the desired answer.

<a id="pm-h-8"></a>
###### Paying for recursive queries.

A wide search or an optimization step may inspect many actions, but it reuses previously gathered child values. Only shared group samples, selected rounded actions and actual online draws require child values at the current refinement index. Common rounded grids limit the number of these calls to slightly more than the tree’s branching factor. Along a dependency path, a call either descends the tree at the same index or decreases an index or pass. Counting these two kinds of steps bounds the total expected work, including rational arithmetic and exact sampling, by $N^{1+o(1)}$.

Section <a href="#sec:geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:geometry">2</a> fixes the computational model, geometry and parameters. Sections <a href="#sec:seed" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:seed">3</a>–<a href="#sec:bands" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:bands">5</a> construct the tables. Sections <a href="#sec:comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:comparison">6</a> and <a href="#sec:regret" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:regret">7</a> prove the geometric and probabilistic estimates, and Section <a href="#sec:accuracy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:accuracy">8</a> assembles the accuracy guarantee. Sections <a href="#sec:numerics" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:numerics">9</a> and <a href="#sec:work" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:work">10</a> implement every operation and complete the running-time proof.

<a id="sec:geometry"></a>
### Alignment geometry and computational parameters

This section fixes the input conventions and the interval states used throughout the algorithm. It also records the geometric inequalities that allow child intervals to be combined even when their target endpoints do not agree.

<a id="pm-h-10"></a>
#### Paths, states and connection costs

Index string boundaries starting at zero. An alignment path has steps $(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$, of cost one, one, and the indicator that the two characters on a diagonal step differ. Such a path gives an edit sequence. Conversely, the original characters that survive an edit sequence occur in the final string in their original order. Deleting other original characters, inserting the remaining output characters and changing each surviving character whose label differs gives an alignment of no greater cost. Thus minimum alignment cost equals edit distance.

For an interval $I=(l,u]$ of the first string, an interval state is $(I,q)$, where $q=(q^-,q^+)$ is an integer pair with $0\le q^-\le q^+\le |y|$. When $I$ is fixed, we also call $q$ a state. Set $$c(I,q)=\operatorname{ED}\bigl(x_{(l,u]},y_{(q^-,q^+]}\bigr),\qquad
 z(I,q)=(q^+-q^-)-(u-l).$$ An endpoint’s *shift* is its target index minus its first-string index. In particular, $z$ is the change in shift between the two endpoints. For pairs use $|q-r|_1=|q^--r^-|+|q^+-r^+|$.

<a id="stmt-lem-geometry"></a>
<div id="lem:geometry" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:connection"></a>
<a id="eq:shift-connection"></a>
**Lemma 2**. *For every interval state, $c(I,q)\ge |z(I,q)|$. Both $c(I,\cdot)$ and $|z(I,\cdot)|$ are $1$-Lipschitz in the endpoint metric. If $I$ is partitioned, in order, into $I_1,\ldots,I_m$, and $\alpha=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)$ is any list of valid child states, define $$\operatorname{conn}_r(\alpha)=|s_1^--r^-|
   +\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}|s_{i+1}^--s_i^+|+|s_m^+-r^+|.$$ Then $$\begin{aligned}
 c(I,r)&\le\sum_i c(I_i,s_i)+\operatorname{conn}_r(\alpha),\label{eq:connection}\\
 |z(I,r)|&\le\sum_i|z(I_i,s_i)|+\operatorname{conn}_r(\alpha).
 \label{eq:shift-connection}
\end{aligned}$$ The connection inequalities also hold for finite target intervals in any extension of $y$ beyond its stored endpoints.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-geometry"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-geometry</summary>

*Proof.* Only insertions and deletions change length, proving $c\ge|z|$. Changing a target substring’s endpoints costs at most $|q-r|_1$: remove or insert endpoint portions if the substrings overlap, and delete and insert the whole substrings if they are disjoint. The triangle inequality gives the claim for $c$; the claim for $|z|$ follows from its formula.

Edit each child to its specified target substring and concatenate the results. Consider the walk on the target’s boundary line that starts at $r^-$, jumps to $s_1^-$, traverses each child target forward, makes the successive connecting jumps, and ends at $r^+$. Expand each jump into unit steps. From this walk choose, in order, one forward crossing of every unit interval between $r^-$ and $r^+$. Successive first arrivals at the next boundary give such a choice. The letters on these selected crossings, in their walk order, form exactly the parent’s target substring. Delete the letters on unselected child crossings, and insert the letters on selected connecting crossings. By net displacement, the number of unselected forward crossings equals the number of backward crossings. All backward crossings belong to connecting jumps, since child targets are traversed forward. Thus deletions cost at most the total backward jump length, while insertions cost at most the total forward jump length. Their sum is $\operatorname{conn}_r(\alpha)$, proving <a href="#eq:connection" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:connection">[eq:connection]</a>. This argument uses only the letters at finitely many target positions, so it also proves the assertion for extensions of $y$. Finally, sum the signed shift changes of child intervals and connecting jumps and take absolute values to obtain <a href="#eq:shift-connection" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:shift-connection">[eq:shift-connection]</a>. ◻

</details>

Figure <a href="#fig:connection-cost" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="fig:connection-cost">1</a> illustrates why the connection term permits both gaps and overlaps between consecutive child targets.

<figure id="fig:connection-cost">

<figcaption>Connection charges for three consecutive source children. Solid arrows show their prescribed target intervals; dashed arrows join these intervals in child order, with the outside endpoints $r = (0,10)$. The jump from $4$ to $3$ points backward, so this walk is not itself an alignment path. Lemma <a href="#lem:geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:geometry">2</a> gives $c(I,r)\le\sum_{i=1}^3c(I_i,s_i)+4$. Only the horizontal target-coordinate displacement of a dashed arrow is charged; the vertical separation of rows is for display.</figcaption>
</figure>

<a id="pm-h-11"></a>
#### Uniform access to the accuracy input

The rational accuracy is supplied in a fixed canonical binary encoding of its positive numerator and denominator in lowest terms, on a separate read-only input. For example, encode a positive integer by its binary length in unary, a delimiter, and its binary digits, and concatenate the two encodings. The input is promised to specify $0<\varepsilon<1$. Prefix inspection is ordinary input access; no numerical operation on the rational is free.

The algorithm first handles equality, empty strings and $|x|\le1$ exactly. These cases require $O(N+1)$ string work. On other inputs define $H$ as the least power of two at least $\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil$, and $\ell$ as the least power of two at least $\max(1,\log_2 H)$. Inspect at most $H^2+O(1)$ bits of the accuracy input. If its complete encoding has not been obtained, use exact alignment dynamic programming. The unread suffix is neither copied nor addressed. All addresses actually used for this prefix have $O(\log(N+2))$ bits. If the encoding is obtained, its integers have $O(H^2)$ bits, and exact arithmetic decides the test $\ell\varepsilon\ge10$ with polynomial work in $H$.

Use exact dynamic programming also if $\ell<2^{1000}$ or $\ell\varepsilon<10$. It uses $O((N+1)^2)$ word operations and can store only two rows. Together with the bounded parameter inspection, this charges every operation in these branches. For each fixed rational encoding, the inspection bound eventually exceeds its length, and both numeric tests eventually pass as $N$ grows. Thus the exact branches affect only a bounded range of $N$ for each fixed $\varepsilon$. They preserve the uniform algorithm and its approximation guarantee on that range. No assertion about efficient joint dependence on encoding length or $1/\varepsilon$ is needed.

<a id="pm-h-12"></a>
#### Parameters and the fixed interval tree

All remaining arguments concern the large-input branch. Logarithms with subscript two are binary, and $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm. The coarse estimator and interval tree use the branching factors $B$ and $M$ below. The factor $A_{\rm init}$ is the initial seed accuracy, $F$ controls its reduction across passes, and $P$ controls endpoint-grid resolution: $$\begin{aligned}
 p_*&=\left\lfloor(\log_2\ell)^{1/4}\right\rfloor,
 &B&=H^{p_*},&A_{\rm init}&=H^{p_*+4},\\
 M&=2^{\lfloor(\log_2 H)/20\rfloor},
 &P&=H^{p_*+20},&F&=\ell.
\end{aligned}$$ The counts $T$ and $S$ govern preliminary propagation and refinement iterations, respectively. The slopes $L_0$ and $L$ penalize changes in target endpoints: $$T=2^{\lceil(3/4)\log_2H\rceil},\qquad S=H/\ell^2,
 \qquad L_0=32F,\qquad L=128F.$$ Finally, fix the error tolerances and the sampling and optimization parameters. Their roles are specified at the corresponding constructions: $$\begin{aligned}
 \delta&=\ell^{-10},&\kappa&=\tau=\ell^{-4},
 &\theta&=\ell^{-40},\\
 \gamma&=\ell^{-20},&\eta&=\ell^5,&Q_1&=\ell^{80}.
\end{aligned}$$ The essential separation is between $H=\Theta(\log(N+2))$ and $\ell=\Theta(\log H)$: the branching factors and grid resolutions are powers of $H$, while the tolerances are powers of $\ell$. The inequalities below quantify the slack available between these scales.

Every integer parameter here is computable using bit lengths and integer tests. For example, $p_*$ is the largest integer whose fourth power is at most the integer $\log_2\ell$. The displayed fractional powers and logarithms require no real-arithmetic oracle. All parameters used as dyadic grid spacings are powers of two, and $S$ is a positive integer in this branch.

We will repeatedly use the generous bounds <a id="eq:parameter-slack"></a>$$\label{eq:parameter-slack}
 H\ge2^{\ell/2},\qquad \ell^{200}\le H^{1/100},\qquad
 p_*+21\le\sqrt\ell.$$ The first follows from the definition of $\ell$; the other two follow at $\ell\ge2^{1000}$ and become stronger as $\ell$ increases. More explicitly, $200\log_2\ell\le\ell/200$ and $(\log_2\ell)^{1/4}+21\le\sqrt\ell$ hold at this cutoff, and their right sides thereafter grow faster. Factors polynomial in $\ell$ and $p_*$ will consequently be much smaller than any fixed positive power of $H$ needed below.

Partition $x$ into a complete $M$-ary tree of height $$J=\left\lceil\log_M\max(1,|x|)\right\rceil.$$ At a node $(l,u]$ use cuts $l_i=l+\lfloor i(u-l)/M\rfloor$, $0\le i\le M$. Empty intervals are allowed, and node labels distinguish repeated intervals. Nodes need only be generated when requested. At depth $j$ the width is at most $\lceil|x|/M^j\rceil$, and leaves have width at most one. The parameters give <a id="eq:tree-bounds"></a>$$\label{eq:tree-bounds}
 J\le100H/\ell,\qquad M^J\le M\max(1,|x|).$$ Indeed $\log_2M\ge (\log_2H)/20-1$ and $\log_2H\ge\ell/2$, whereas $\log_2|x|\le H$. The second bound follows directly from the ceiling defining $J$.

At a leaf of width zero the exact cost is the target length. At a leaf containing one character, the cost is one for an empty target, and otherwise is the target length minus the indicator that this character occurs there. Sort the pairs (symbol, position) of $y$ lexicographically by comparison sorting. A binary search then tests occurrence in any target interval in $O(\log(N+2))$ time, with $O(N\log(N+2))$ preprocessing work and linear storage. The word-label assumption makes each comparison a bounded number of word operations. Fresh padding symbols used later can be represented by a tag together with a label; no search for an unused alphabet value is needed.

All subsequent tables are indexed by this fixed tree and valid endpoint pairs. The total domain is polynomial in $N+2$: there are at most $2M^J$ nodes and at most $(|y|+1)^2$ pairs per node. A simultaneous probability guarantee over this domain is meaningful even though the algorithm will evaluate only a small part of it.

<a id="sec:seed"></a>
### Simultaneous coarse estimates

The refinement will need an integer estimate at every interval state, including states chosen adaptively by later computations. We construct these estimates as a random table, while evaluating only the entries that are requested. The construction builds on tree and precision-sampling ideas of Andoni, Krauthgamer, and Onak (Andoni, Krauthgamer, and Onak 2010) <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[AndoniKrauthgamerOnak2010](#ref-AndoniKrauthgamerOnak2010)]; the complete bounds needed here are proved below.

<a id="stmt-thm-seed"></a>
<div id="thm:seed" class="theorem">

<a id="eq:seed-guarantee"></a>
**Theorem 3** (Initial estimates). *With the parameters and labeled interval tree of Section <a href="#sec:geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:geometry">2</a>, there is a lazily evaluated random table $U^{(0)}(I,q)$ of integers in $[0,N]$ such that, with probability at least $0.99$, simultaneously at every state, $$\label{eq:seed-guarantee}
